BILLIONS OF YEARS
For thousands of years,
humanity found solace in a single,
comforting assumption: the universe
is a masterfully crafted clockwork mechanism.
From Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas
to Sir Isaac Newton,
many of the greatest thinkers saw
a divine mind behind the order of nature.
They argued that every rolling
stone, every falling drop of rain,
and every orbiting planet followed
a predetermined order.
But what if the bedrock of reality
is not a clockwork at all?
What if, at the deepest level,
the universe runs on pure chance?
Today, we look into quantum physics
to ask what it can,
and cannot, tell us about that question.
Before we begin, a note on what
this video is.
Physics describes how particles behave.
Whether that says anything about
God is a philosophical question,
and thoughtful people disagree about it.
We will follow one line of argument
through real experiments, and we
will mark where the facts end and
interpretation begins.
Throughout much of classical
history, theology and physics walked
hand in hand under the banner of determinism.
Classical physics assured us that
if you possessed the exact
coordinates and momentum of every
particle, the entire future could
be calculated with flawless certainty.
Many took this predictability as
a fingerprint of God,
a sign that a supreme mind charted
the cosmos from beginning to end.
Yet, at the dawn of the twentieth
century, human curiosity cracked
open the subatomic realm,
and that classical certainty began to crumble.
In nineteen twenty-seven, the most
brilliant minds on Earth gathered
in Brussels, Belgium, for the Solvay
Conference, to argue over the
meaning of the new quantum theory.
On one side stood Albert Einstein,
the ultimate defender of cosmic
order, who believed the universe
must be governed by strict rational laws.
On the other stood Niels Bohr and
a cadre of young,
radical physicists who had uncovered
something strange beneath the fabric
of reality.
Einstein famously objected: God
does not play dice with the universe!
Bohr is said to have answered:
Stop telling God what to do.
A foundational experiment of quantum
physics is the double-slit experiment.
When physicists fired solid
particles of matter, electrons,
through two narrow barriers,
they expected two neat lines to
appear on the detector screen.
Instead, what materialized was
a stunning interference pattern
of alternating light and dark bands,
the unmistakable signature of a wave.
How could solid, discrete units
of matter behave like rippling
waves in an ocean?
The pattern builds up even when
electrons are sent one at a time,
as if each single electron passes
through both slits at once,
interfering with its own ghost.
Stunned by this impossibility,
researchers placed microscopic
detectors at the slits to observe
which path the electron actually chose.
And that is when reality revealed
its deeply disturbing, almost
paranormal secret.
The moment an observation was made,
the interference pattern vanished.
The electron stopped acting like
a spread-out wave and behaved like
a single point particle,
creating two plain lines.
The mere act of measurement
fundamentally changed the outcome.
In the standard interpretation,
this is called the collapse of
the wave function, and it suggests
that subatomic reality has no
definite state until it is measured.
In nineteen twenty-seven, German
physicist Werner Heisenberg
formulated a cornerstone of quantum
theory: the Uncertainty Principle.
Heisenberg showed that it is
physically impossible to
simultaneously know the exact
position and the exact momentum
of a subatomic particle.
The more precisely you pin down
where an electron is,
the more unpredictable its momentum becomes.
This is not a limitation of human
technology, nor is it a temporary
flaw in our laboratory equipment.
It is an intrinsic law woven into
the fabric of the cosmos itself.
In standard quantum theory,
the universe sets an absolute
barrier on what can be known about
a particle at once.
Consider the radioactive decay
of an unstable atom,
such as carbon-fourteen or
uranium-two-thirty-eight.
You can calculate the half-life
of a vast collection of such atoms
with extraordinary statistical accuracy.
You know that within a specific
timeframe, half of them will decay.
But if you ask:
Why did this specific atom decay
at this exact microsecond while
its neighbor remained completely stable?
Standard quantum mechanics gives
a shocking answer: There is no reason.
There is no internal clock ticking
down, and no hidden cause that
anyone has ever found.
The timing appears to be fundamentally random.
Some physicists explore theories
with hidden variables, but
experiments have not revealed any.
Perhaps the most staggering
discovery of modern quantum field
theory is that the vacuum of empty
space is not actually empty.
If you strip away every star,
every atom, and every photon of
radiation, the remaining void still
seethes with activity.
In a common popular picture,
based on the uncertainty relation
between energy and time,
particles borrow energy from
nothingness, pop into existence
for a tiny fraction of a second,
and vanish again.
Their effects are measured in
precision laboratories through
phenomena like the Casimir effect
and the Lamb shift.
As if random decay were not
unsettling enough, the role of
the observer plunges physics into
an even deeper puzzle.
In the standard Copenhagen
interpretation of quantum mechanics,
subatomic systems exist in a blend
of overlapping possibilities called
a superposition.
An electron is spinning up and
down at the same time,
until a measurement forces it into
a single definite result.
This raises a paradox that haunted
early quantum pioneers: Does the
universe exist when no one is watching?
If reality requires measurement
to become definite, what was
measuring the cosmos during the
billions of years before life emerged?
Decoherence offers a partial answer.
Whenever a quantum system interacts
with its wider environment,
whether by colliding with a stray
photon or bumping into a single
gas molecule, its fragile quantum
coherence leaks irreversibly into
the surroundings.
The ghostly superposition becomes
impossible to detect, and the system
behaves like classical, solid reality.
Even a speck of dust drifting
through deep space is constantly
struck by the faint glow of cosmic
microwave radiation.
In this picture, no conscious
observer is needed to make the
world look definite; the environment
does that work automatically.
But decoherence does not by itself
explain why we see one single
outcome, and physicists still debate that.
In nineteen thirty-five, Albert
Einstein, along with Boris Podolsky
and Nathan Rosen, argued that
quantum mechanics must be
incomplete, in what became known
as the EPR Paradox.
They pointed out that if quantum
theory were true, two particles
could become entangled, linked
so intimately that measuring one
would instantly fix the state of
the other, however far apart they were.
Einstein later dismissed this as
spooky action at a distance,
convinced that it clashed with
the idea that nothing can influence
anything else faster than light.
For three decades, the scientific
world remained in philosophical deadlock.
Did the particles carry hidden,
pre-programmed instructions given
to them at birth,
what physicists call local hidden variables?
Or was reality fundamentally
nonlocal, interconnected in a way
no classical picture allows?
In nineteen sixty-four, a brilliant
Northern Irish physicist named
John Stewart Bell changed the debate
by formulating a mathematical test:
Bell's Inequality.
Bell proved that if the classical,
commonsense worldview held by
Einstein were correct, experimental
measurements could never exceed
a strict statistical limit.
If that limit were broken,
no theory that was both local and
realistic could be right.
In the early nineteen eighties,
Alain Aspect carried out landmark
experiments, and increasingly
airtight loophole-closing tests
followed in later decades.
In twenty twenty-two, Aspect,
John Clauser, and Anton Zeilinger
shared the Nobel Prize in Physics
for their experiments with entangled
photons that established the
violation of Bell's Inequality.
The verdict was clear:
the inequality was violated,
again and again.
Local realism failed the test.
This means either physical objects
do not possess definite properties
prior to measurement, or distant
particles are linked in a way no
local mechanism can explain.
Importantly, this link cannot be
used to send messages faster than light.
The neat, localized universe of
classical causality does not
describe our world.
Another famous reading of quantum
theory is the Many-Worlds Interpretation.
Proposed by Hugh Everett the Third
in nineteen fifty-seven, it takes
the mathematics of the Schrödinger
equation completely seriously
without adding a collapse mechanism.
Everett dared to ask:
What if the wave function never
collapses at all?
What if, every time a quantum event
has multiple possible outcomes,
all of those outcomes actually
occur in branching parallel realities?
If Everett is right,
reality is not a single,
curated terrarium built for mankind,
but an unfathomable, ever-branching
multiverse.
It remains one interpretation among
several, and it cannot yet be tested directly.
In nineteen sixty-one, the physicist
Eugene Wigner, who would later
win a Nobel Prize,
introduced a mind-bending thought
experiment known as Wigner's Friend.
Imagine a physicist inside an
isolated laboratory measuring a
quantum particle.
To the friend inside,
the measurement is complete,
and the wave function has collapsed
to a single definitive result.
But to Wigner, standing outside
the sealed laboratory, the entire
room, including his friend,
remains in an entangled
superposition until Wigner opens the door!
Laboratory tests with entangled
photons have been reported to
support a version of this idea,
suggesting that two observers may
not always agree on a single set of facts.
The modern quest for ultimate truth
has driven physicists to attempt
the holy grail of science:
unifying Einstein's General
Relativity with Quantum Mechanics
into a Theory of Everything.
Einstein described gravity as the
smooth, continuous curvature of
space and time, a pristine geometric
cathedral.
But when you zoom into the Planck
scale, the fabric of spacetime
may stop being smooth.
It is thought to dissolve into
Quantum Foam, a boiling sea where
space and time fluctuate wildly,
perhaps even twisting into
microscopic wormholes in some
speculative models.
At that scale, the classical concept
of time may break down.
When physicists John Wheeler and
Bryce DeWitt combined quantum theory
with the geometry of the universe,
they produced the famous
Wheeler-DeWitt Equation.
What stands out is what is missing
from the equation: the variable
for time, represented by the letter
t, has vanished.
The master equation of the universe
reads: H-psi equals zero.
Some physicists read this to mean
that, at the most fundamental level,
time may not flow,
and that the time we experience
may emerge from quantum entanglement.
This remains a hypothesis,
not a settled result.
We cannot discuss quantum theology
without confronting Erwin
Schrödinger's infamous thought
experiment: Schrödinger's Cat.
Devised in nineteen thirty-five
to illustrate the sheer absurdity
of the Copenhagen interpretation,
the setup is brutally simple.
A cat is placed in a steel
box with a radioactive atom,
a Geiger counter, a vial of poison,
and a hammer.
If the atom decays,
the hammer drops, the poison
shatters, and the cat dies.
If the atom does not decay,
the cat lives.
Taken literally, the Copenhagen
reading says that until the box
is opened, the atom is in a
superposition of both decayed and undecayed.
Therefore, the cat would be both
dead and alive!
Schrödinger meant this as a
criticism, not as a prediction.
What, then, is the fundamental
nature of the cosmos revealed by
quantum physics?
Pioneering theoretical physicist
John Archibald Wheeler coined the
legendary phrase: It from Bit.
He proposed that all physical
entities, matter, radiation, forces,
and spacetime itself, are ultimately
derived from information.
Some physicists suspect that the
bedrock of reality is not solid
clay but quantum bits,
qubits, processing through
entanglement and superposition.
On this view, the cosmos behaves
like an emergent quantum computation

It remains a speculative idea.
We arrive at the precipice of understanding.
For millennia, people have looked
